title: Voice AI basics
goal: Know how a voice agent works end to end, and what each RevRag setting changes.
kickoff: 1-hour kickoff at the start of week 2
learn: Draw the speech-to-text → LLM → text-to-speech loop and explain each step
Explain why latency matters and how streaming helps
Explain turn-taking and interruptions, and which settings control them
Place each RevRag settings tab on the call

concepts.title: Every reply goes ears → brain → mouth
concepts.summary: Speech-to-text, then the LLM, then text-to-speech, then the loop starts again.
body: The ears: speech-to-text (STT) turns the caller's voice into written text.
The brain: the LLM reads the text, follows its prompt and writes a reply.
The mouth: text-to-speech (TTS) turns the reply into a natural-sounding voice.
The reply plays back to the caller and the loop starts again. Every step takes time, and the delays add up.

concepts.title: Why speed matters: waiting vs streaming
concepts.summary: One step at a time adds up to ~1.9 s of silence. Streaming overlaps the steps so the first word comes at ~0.6 s.
body: One step at a time: STT 0.5 s + LLM 1.0 s + TTS 0.4 s, and the caller waits 1.9 s for the first word.
Streaming: the LLM writes word by word and TTS starts speaking before the reply is done, so the first word arrives at about 0.6 s.
About 0.4 to 0.8 s feels natural. Past 1 to 2 s, callers talk over the agent.
Timings are illustrative.

concepts.title: Turn-taking: has the caller finished?
concepts.summary: A silence timer decides when it's the agent's turn. Too short cuts people off; too long feels slow.
body: People pause mid-sentence all the time, so the agent has to guess when they've finished.
Timer too short: the agent jumps in during a natural pause and cuts the caller off.
Timer too long: every reply starts late and the agent feels slow and robotic.
Smart turn detection also reads the words: "for my…" isn't finished yet. In RevRag this lives in the Speech tab: turn detection and response eagerness.

concepts.title: Interruptions: when the caller cuts in
concepts.summary: Barge-in means the agent stops the moment the caller talks. Noise and echo cause false alarms.
body: Barge-in: the agent stops the moment the caller starts talking, then listens. In RevRag: the interruption settings.
False alarms: a cough, a TV or street noise can look like an interruption. In RevRag: background noise.
Echo: the agent's own voice leaking back into the mic can sound like the caller cutting in.
Many complaints about agents that keep stopping or won't stop talking come down to these settings.

concepts.title: Where LiveKit fits
concepts.summary: A LiveKit room is like a Zoom call. Your agent is a program that joins it and runs STT → LLM → TTS.
body: You join the room from a browser (P2), or a phone call is connected into it through SIP (week 3).
Your agent program, Python from the quickstart, joins the same room as another participant.
It listens, sends the audio through STT, the LLM and TTS (AI services reached over the internet) and speaks back into the room.

concepts.title: The RevRag agent settings, placed on the call
concepts.summary: For each setting, ask which step of the call it changes: before, hear, think, speak or after.
body: Before the call: Pre-call processing gets things ready, like the lead's details.
Hear: the Speech tab, with the STT model, turn detection, interruption, response eagerness and background noise.
Think: the LLM model, the knowledge base and functions: which model thinks, what it knows and the actions it can take.
Speak: Voice and Pronunciation, how it sounds and how it says names and words.
After the call: Post-call processing, with summaries and outcomes sent on to the client's systems.
Across every step: Fallbacks, the backup plan for when something goes wrong.

concepts.title: Why P1 and P2? In week 3 they join up
concepts.summary: When a call with your bot ends, P2 sends a signed summary to P1. RevRag does the same for clients every day.
body: Your practice in week 3 (P3): when a call with your bot ends, the bot sends a summary to your app by webhook, signed with a shared secret.
Real client work: when a campaign call ends, RevRag sends the result to the client's CRM by webhook, signed and checked the same way.
Learn the pattern on your own projects first, then do it for real clients.

projects.title: Your own voice bot
projects.summary: The ears → brain → mouth loop, built with the LiveKit Voice AI quickstart and your own prompt.
steps: Create a free LiveKit Cloud account, then follow the Voice AI quickstart with Claude Code.
Give the bot a short prompt for a real use case, such as qualifying a loan lead.
Talk to it in the browser. Change one setting at a time (voice, turn detection, interruption) and note what each change does.
Push the code and your prompt to a GitHub repo in your own account.
projects.done_when: You can hold a 2-minute conversation with the bot, and you have notes on 3 setting changes.

submit.label: Link to a screen recording of a 2-minute conversation
Notes on 3 setting changes: what you changed, what you expected, what happened

projects.warning: Keep your LiveKit keys in .env and out of the repo.

quiz.question: What is the correct order of the voice agent loop?
Why does streaming make a voice agent feel faster?
options: The steps overlap, so TTS starts speaking before the full reply is written
quiz.explanation: Each step works on partial results, so the first word arrives in well under a second instead of ~1.9 s.

quiz.question: Roughly how quickly should the first word of a reply arrive to feel natural?
options: It doesn't matter on a phone call
quiz.explanation: About 0.4 to 0.8 s feels natural. Past 1 to 2 s, callers start talking over the agent.

quiz.question: A client says their agent keeps cutting callers off mid-sentence. Which setting is the likeliest cause?
options: The turn-detection silence timer is too short
The knowledge base is too big
quiz.explanation: A timer that's too short makes the agent jump in during natural pauses. In RevRag it lives in the Speech tab.

quiz.question: The agent keeps stopping mid-sentence even though the caller is silent. Which of these could cause it?
options: The LLM prompt is too short
Background noise or echo being mistaken for the caller
The caller's phone is on Wi-Fi
quiz.explanation: Noise and echo cause false barge-ins. Check the background noise and interruption settings.

quiz.question: Sending a call summary to the client's CRM belongs to which settings area?
quiz.explanation: After the call: post-call processing sends summaries and outcomes on to the client's systems.

quiz.question: In LiveKit, how does your agent take part in a call?
options: It joins the room as another participant
It records the call and replies later
It runs inside the caller's browser tab
quiz.explanation: The agent is just another participant in the room, like a person joining a Zoom call.

quiz.question: STT takes 0.5 s, the LLM 1.0 s and TTS 0.4 s, one after another. How long until the caller hears the first word?
quiz.explanation: Without streaming the delays add up: 0.5 + 1.0 + 0.4 = 1.9 s of silence.

quiz.question: What does smart turn detection add on top of a silence timer?
options: It makes the agent's voice louder
It also reads the words to judge whether the sentence is finished
quiz.explanation: "For my…" isn't a finished sentence, so the agent keeps listening even if there's a pause.

quiz.question: What is barge-in?
options: The agent stops talking the moment the caller starts
The agent transfers the call to a person
The caller is put on hold
The agent talks over the caller
quiz.explanation: A good agent notices the caller's voice, stops almost at once, and listens.

quiz.question: Which settings tab controls how the agent says names and unusual words?
quiz.explanation: Speak: Voice and Pronunciation decide how it sounds and how it says names and words.

quiz.question: In week 3, how will your P1 app know a webhook really came from your P2 bot?
options: It comes from a Vercel address
The request is signed with a shared secret
It uses GET instead of POST
quiz.explanation: A signature made with a shared secret (HMAC) proves the sender, the same way RevRag signs client webhooks.

quiz.question: What are Fallbacks for?
options: The backup plan for when something goes wrong during a call
quiz.explanation: Fallbacks span every step of the call: they decide what happens when something fails.

quiz.question: Which part of a voice agent follows the prompt and decides what to say?
quiz.explanation: The brain is the LLM: it reads the transcribed text, follows its prompt and writes the reply.

voice_quiz.prompt: Describe the ears, brain and mouth of a voice agent, and what each one does.
look_for: the LLM follows the prompt and writes a reply
text-to-speech turns the reply into a voice

voice_quiz.prompt: Why does latency matter so much for voice agents, and how does streaming help?

first word around 0.4 to 0.8 seconds feels natural
callers talk over a slow agent

voice_quiz.prompt: A client says the agent feels slow and robotic, but also sometimes cuts people off. Talk me through turn detection and what you'd change.
look_for: smart turn detection reads the words
